Colleagues 4,5,7 argue for Case 1 and Case 3 using the non-parametric residual $D-E[D\mid X]$; that is a sign-protected partial effect but not the linear projection $Y\sim1+D+X$ under unrestricted $m_0(\cdot),p(\cdot)$. The correct population OLS sign requirement is therefore only Case 1, option A. Unresolved nuance: if the researcher were allowed a fully flexible control of $X$, Case 3 would be sign-protected; the problem explicitly asks for the linear control.
reflection_text.1:
The problem is sign of the population OLS coefficient on D in three designs with Y=Y0+Dτ, τ_i>0 a.s., under unconfoundedness.

Case 1. D⊥(Y0,Y1). Then β1 = E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y1]-E[Y0]=E[τ]>0. Unconditional randomisation is sign-protected. All colleagues agree.

Case 2. D⊥(Y0,Y1)|X but D≠⊥X in general. 
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[E[Y1|X]|D=1]-E[E[Y0|X]|D=0]
= E[τ|X,D=1]+E[μ0(X)|D=1]-E[μ0(X)|D=0].
Conditional mean difference E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=E[τ|X]>0 pointwise, but the marginal difference contains selection bias E[μ0(X)|D=1]-E[μ0(X)|D=0]. With p(X)=P(D=1|X) monotone opposite to μ0(X) the bias can dominate the positive τ term. Example X∈{0,1}, p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1, μ0(0)=0, μ0(1)=M, τ=ε>0 gives E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=ε-0.8M<0 for large M. Hence the uncontrolled regression Y~1+D is not sign-protected under conditional randomisation. This is consensus.

Case 3. D⊥(Y0,Y1)|X and we run linear projection Y=α+β3 D+γ X+ε.
Write μ0(X)=E[Y0|X], τ(X)=E[τ|X]>0, p(X)=E[D|X], v(X)=p(1-p). 
Conditional on X, Cov(Y,D|X)=τ(X)v(X)>0.
If X were controlled nonparametrically, the coefficient would be
β* = E[τ(X)v(X)]/E[v(X)]>0, a positive weighted average of τ(X). 
That is the argument used by colleagues 4,5,7.

With a linear control, β3 = Cov(Y, D⊥)/Var(D⊥) where D⊥=D-Π_{1,X}D is the residual from the linear projection of D on 1,X. Then
E[D⊥Y|X]=E[D⊥|X]μ0(X)+E[D⊥D|X]τ(X)
and E[D⊥|X]=p(X)-a0-a1X≠0 in general. Hence
Cov(Y,D⊥)=E[(p(X)-a0-a1X)μ0(X)]+E[τ(X)E[D⊥D|X]].
The second term is >0 but the first term is Cov of the non-linear part of p(X) with μ0(X). With non-linear p(·) and non-linear μ0(·) the first term can be made arbitrarily negative and dominate the positive second term. Concrete counter-examples are given with X∈{-1,0,1}, p(-1)=0.2,p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.3, μ0(x)=x², τ≡0.1, leading to β3<0. Likewise with Cov(D,X)=0 one can get β3 negative. So linear projection on 1,D,X does not inherit the sign of E[τ|X]>0.

The disagreement in the round is precisely this point: colleagues 4,5,7 compute Cov(Y, D-E[D|X]) and treat the linear residual as D-E[D|X]. That is correct for the non-parametric control of X, not for the linear control specified. Once the projection is restricted to the linear span {1,X}, orthogonality to μ0(X) is lost unless μ0 and p are linear in X.

Hence under the stated non-parametric assumptions beyond positivity of τ, sign is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation. Conditional randomisation protects the conditional mean difference but not the marginal OLS slope in Case 2 nor the linear partial slope in Case 3. My current belief is A. Only Case 1.

7.text:
The population OLS coefficient is the coefficient of the $L^{2}$ linear
projection of $Y$ on the regressors that are included.

Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau=Y(1)-Y(0)>0$ a.s., and with conditional
unconfoundedness

$E[Y\mid X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$,      $m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$,
$\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$,               $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$.

Case 1. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0),Y(1))$.
\[
\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)]-E[Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0 .
\]
Unconditional randomisation is the ATE. The sign is forced.

Case 2. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ but in general
$D\not\perp\!\!\!\perp X$.  Then
\[
E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
 =E[\tau\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0].
\]
The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ can be made
arbitrarily negative by letting $p(X)$ be decreasing in $m_{0}(X)$. With
$\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$ arbitrarily small,
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=\varepsilon+{\rm bias}$ can be $<0$.  Conditional
unconfoundedness does not imply marginal unconfoundedness.

Case 3. The regression is the linear projection on $\{1,D,X\}$.
Put $D_{\perp}=D-\Pi_{1,X}D$, the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$.
Then
\[
\beta_{3}= \frac{{\rm Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})}{{\rm Var}(D_{\perp})}
        =\frac{E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]+E[\tau(X)D D_{\perp}]}
               {E[D_{\perp}^{2}]} .
\]
$E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]>0$ but $E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]=
E\big[(p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X)m_{0}(X)\big]$ is generally non-zero.
$D_{\perp}$ is orthogonal in $L^{2}$ to $1,X$ only, not to an arbitrary
function of $X$. With a non-linear $m_{0}(\cdot)$ and a non-linear
propensity $p(\cdot)$ the residual $p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X$ can be correlated
with $m_{0}(X)$ with a sign opposite to the positive $\tau$-term and with
arbitrarily large magnitude by scaling $m_{0}$. Hence
${\rm Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})$ can be made negative even though
${\rm Cov}(Y,D\mid X)=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D\mid X)>0$ pointwise.

E.g. $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$, $p(-1)=0.2$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.3$,
$m_{0}(x)=x^{2}$, $\tau(x)\equiv0.1>0$ gives $E[D_{\perp}Y]<0$ and
$\beta_{3}<0$.  The same construction works for any $c>0$.

Thus $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ a.s., but the best
linear predictor of $Y$ on $1,D,X$ is not the non-parametric
regression coefficient $E[\tau(X)w(X)]/E[w(X)]$ with $w(X)=p(X)(1-p(X))$.
The linear misspecification of $E[D\mid X]$ and $E[Y(0)\mid X]$ allows
sign reversal.

Positivity of the population $D$ coefficient is therefore guaranteed only
by unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can be negative with
$\tau_{i}>0$ a.s.

A. Only Case 1.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection of $Y$ on the regressors included.

Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$ with $\tau_i>0$ a.s. and under conditional randomisation
$D\perp (Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ so that
$E[Y\mid D,X]=m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$ with $m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$ and
$\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$.

Case 1. $D\perp (Y(0),Y(1))$, hence $D\perp X$ and
$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
The intercept-slope projection is the mean difference, the ATE, and is
strictly positive.

Case 2. $D\perp (Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$ in general.
$$
\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
      =E[\tau\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0].
$$
$E[\tau\mid D=1]>0$ but the selection term can dominate. With
$X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=P(D=1\mid X=0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(0)=0$,
$m_{0}(1)=M$ and $\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$,
$\beta_{2}= \varepsilon-0.8M<0$ for $M$ large. Uncontrolled $Y\sim D$ is not sign protected.

Case 3. Projection on $\{1,D,X\}$ is $\beta_{3}=E[D_{\perp}Y]/E[D_{\perp}^{2}]$
with $D_{\perp}=D-a_{0}-a_{1}X$ the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$.
$$
E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]+E[D_{\perp}D\,\tau(X)] .
$$
$E[D_{\perp}D\,\tau(X)]>0$ but $E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]=E[(p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X)m_{0}(X)]$
is the covariance of the non-linear part of the propensity with the
baseline. With non-linear $p(\cdot)$ and non-linear $m_{0}(\cdot)$ this term
can be made arbitrarily negative. E.g. $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ with equal mass,
$p(-1)=0.2$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.3$, $m_{0}(x)=x^{2}$, $\tau(x)\equiv0.1$,
the linear residual $D_{\perp}$ is negatively correlated with $m_{0}(X)$ and
$E[D_{\perp}Y]<0$, i.e. $\beta_{3}<0$, although $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$
for every $X$.

The sign-protected quantity is the non-parametric partial effect
$E[(D-E[D\mid X])Y]/E[(D-E[D\mid X])^{2}]
=E[\tau(X)w(X)]/E[w(X)]>0$, $w(X)=p(X)(1-p(X))$, which uses the
$X$-conditional residual $D-E[D\mid X]$. That is not the OLS coefficient
with $X$ entered linearly. With only a linear control the $m_{0}(X)$ term
is not removed and can reverse sign.

Hence a strictly positive population OLS coefficient on $D$ is forced only
under unconditional randomisation. That is Case 1.

Option A. Only Case 1.

2.text:
The population OLS coefficient is the coefficient of the linear
projection on the space spanned by the regressors.

Write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau=Y_{1}-Y_{0}>0$ a.s., and under conditional
unconfoundedness
$$
E[Y\mid D,X]=m_{0}(X)+D\, \tau(X),\qquad m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}\mid X],\;
\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0 .
$$

Case 1.  $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})$. Then
$$
\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0,
$$
the usual randomised ATE.  The intercept-slope projection is the mean
difference and its sign is forced.

Case 2.  $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})\mid X$ but $D\not\perp\!\!\!\perp X$.
$$
E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]
-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0].
$$
The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ is
$E[m_{0}(X)p(X)]/E[p(X)]-E[m_{0}(X)(1-p(X))]/E[1-p(X)]$ with
$p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$.  By making $p(X)$ decreasing in $m_{0}(X)$ it can be
made arbitrarily negative and arbitrarily large in absolute value relative
to the bounded positive $E[\tau\mid D=1]$.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$,
$p(0)=0.9,\;p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(0)=0,\;m_{0}(1)=M$, $\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$
gives $\beta_{2}= \varepsilon-0.8M<0$ for $M$ large.  So the marginal
$Y\sim1+D$ projection is not sign protected.

Case 3.  The coefficient from $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+\varepsilon$,
$E[\varepsilon D]=E[\varepsilon X]=0$, is
$$
\beta_{3}= \frac{E[D_{\perp}Y]}{E[D_{\perp}^{2}]},\qquad 
D_{\perp}=D-a_{0}-a_{1}X
$$
the residual of $D$ from its linear projection on $1,X$, not from the
non-parametric projection $D-E[D\mid X]$.  Now
$$
E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]+E[D_{\perp}D\,\tau(X)] .
$$
$E[D_{\perp}D\,\tau(X)]>0$ but
$E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]= \operatorname{Cov}(m_{0}(X),D-a_{0}-a_{1}X)$
is zero only when $m_{0}$ and $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$ are both linear in $X$.
With a non-linear $m_{0}$ and a non-linear $p$ the first term can be made
arbitrarily negative and dominate the second.  With $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$,
$p(-1)=0.2,\;p(0)=0.9,\;p(1)=0.3$, $m_{0}(x)=x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv0.1$, one
gets $E[D_{\perp}Y]<0$, i.e. $\beta_{3}<0$ even though
$E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ a.s.

Hence the population linear projection on $1,D,X$ is not a positive
weighted average of $\tau(X)$; it is a linear approximation to the
non-parametric control.  The non-parametric coefficient
$E[[\tau(X)p(1-p)]]/E[p(1-p)]>0$ would be positive, but that is the
coefficient obtained when $X$ is controlled for non-parametrically, i.e.
with residual $D-E[D\mid X]$, not the OLS coefficient with $X$ entered
linearly.

Unconditional randomisation is therefore the only situation in which
positivity of $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s. forces a strictly positive population OLS
coefficient on $D$.

A. Only Case 1

6.text:
The population OLS coefficient is the coefficient of the linear projection
on the regressors that are actually included.

Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$,
$p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$ and $h(X)=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$ with
$\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$.

*Case 1.* $D\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0),Y(1))$.
\[
\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)]-E[Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0 .
\]
Unconditional randomisation is the ATE and the mean difference is
strictly positive.

*Case 2.* $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ but $D\not\perp\!\!\!\perp X$.
\[
E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]
                -E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0].
\]
The second term is selection on $X$.  With $p(0)=0.9,\;p(1)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(0)=0,\;m_{0}(1)=M$ and $\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$,
\[
E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=\varepsilon-0.8M<0
\]
for $M$ large.  Conditional randomisation does not imply marginal
randomisation.

*Case 3.*  $E[Y\mid D,X]=m_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)$ with $\tau(X)>0$ so that
${\rm Cov}(Y,D\mid X)=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D\mid X)>0$.
The population linear projection on $\{1,D,X\}$ is
\[
\beta_{3}= \frac{E[D_{\perp}Y]}{E[D_{\perp}^{2}]},\qquad
D_{\perp}=D-{\rm proj}_{1,X}(D) .
\]
Write $D_{\perp}=D-a_{0}-a_{1}X$. Then
\[
E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]+E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)] .
\]
The second term is $E[\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))]>0$.  The first term is
$E[(p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X)m_{0}(X)]$, the covariance of the residual of
$p(X)$ from its linear projection on $1,X$ with $m_{0}(X)$.  It is zero
only if $p(X)$ is linear in $X$.  With a non-linear $p(\cdot)$ and a
non-linear $m_{0}(\cdot)$ the first term can be made arbitrarily
negative and dominate the positive $\tau$ part.

E.g. $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ with $P(X=x)=1/3$,
$p(-1)=0.2,\;p(0)=0.8,\;p(1)=0.3$, $m_{0}(x)=x^{2}$, $\tau(x)\equiv0.1>0$.
Then $E[D_{\perp}Y]<0$ and the linear projection
$Y=\alpha+\beta_{3}D+\gamma X+\varepsilon$ has $\beta_{3}<0$ despite
$Y(1)>Y(0)$ a.s. and $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$.

The positive weighted average
$\displaystyle E[\tau(X)w(X)]/E[w(X)]$, $w(X)=p(X)(1-p(X))$,
is the coefficient obtained with the non-parametric residual
$\tilde D=D-E[D\mid X]$, i.e. with a fully non-parametric control for
$X$.  The question asks for the linear control $1,D,X$, for which the
residual is $D-{\rm proj}_{1,X}(D)$.  Under linear misspecification the
sign is not protected.

Hence the population OLS coefficient on $D$ is sign protected only
under unconditional randomisation.  Cases 2 and 3 can be made negative
with $\tau>0$ a.s.

Option A. Only Case 1.

1.text:
The population linear projection is what OLS estimates.

Write $Y = Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $\mu_0(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$,
$\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ and $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$, $v(X)=p(X)(1-p(X))>0$.
Under conditional unconfoundedness
$E[Y|D,X]=\mu_0(X)+D\,\tau(X)$ and ${\rm Cov}(Y,D|X)=\tau(X)v(X)>0$.

Case 1 $D\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0),Y(1))$.  Then
$$
\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)]-E[Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0
$$
is the ATE.  Sign is protected.

Case 2 $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))|X$ but $D\not\perp\!\!\!\perp X$.
$$
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau|D=1]+E[\mu_0(X)|D=1]-E[\mu_0(X)|D=0].
$$
The conditional mean difference $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$,
but the marginal difference contains the selection bias
$E[\mu_0(X)|D=1]-E[\mu_0(X)|D=0]$.  With $p(X)$ monotone opposite to
$\mu_0(X)$ the bias can dominate $\tau$.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$,
$p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $\mu_0(0)=0,\mu_0(1)=M$, $\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$,
gives $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=\varepsilon-0.8M<0$ for $M$ large.  The
uncontrolled $Y\sim1+D$ regression is not sign-protected.

Case 3.  Let $D_{\perp}=D-a_{0}-a_{1}X$ be the residual from the linear
projection of $D$ on $1,X$.  Then
$$
\beta_{3}= \frac{E[D_{\perp}Y]}{E[D_{\perp}^{2}]},\qquad
E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}\mu_0(X)]+E[\tau(X)D_{\perp}D].
$$
Now $E[D_{\perp}D|X]=p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X$ times $v(X)$ up to scale, so
$$
E[\tau(X)D_{\perp}D]=E\!\left[\tau(X) \bigl(p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X\bigr)
      v(X)\right]>0
$$
in the sense of a positive term, but
$$
E[D_{\perp}\mu_0(X)]=E\!\left[\bigl(p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X\bigr)\mu_0(X)\right]
$$
is generally non-zero.  Orthogonality $E[D_{\perp}\mu_0(X)]=0$ holds iff
$p(X)$ is linear in $X$, i.e. iff $E[D|X]$ lies in the span $\{1,X\}$.
With a non-linear propensity and a non-linear $\mu_0$ the first term can
be made arbitrarily negative.

E.g. $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equally likely, $p(-1)=0.2,p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.3$,
$\mu_0(x)=x^{2}$, $\tau(x)\equiv0.1$.  The linear projection of $D$ on
$1,X$ gives $D_{\perp}=D-\hat a_{0}-\hat a_{1}X$ with
$E[D_{\perp}\mu_0(X)]<0$ and $|E[D_{\perp}\mu_0(X)]|$ dominates
$E[\tau(X)D_{\perp}D]>0$, so $\beta_{3}<0$ despite
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ for every $X$.

In other words the non-parametric partial coefficient
$\beta^{*}=E[\tau(X)v(X)]/E[v(X)]>0$ is the sign-protected quantity,
and $\beta^{*}$ is what you get when $X$ is controlled non-parametrically,
i.e. with residual $D-E[D|X]$.  With the linear control $1,X$ the residual
is $D-\Pi_{1,X}D$ and orthogonality to $\mu_0(X)$ is lost.  Hence
unconfoundedness with a strictly positive individual effect does not
imply $\beta_{3}>0$.

Positivity of the population OLS coefficient on $D$ is therefore forced
only under unconditional randomisation.  Cases 2 and 3 are not sign-protected
without further functional-form restrictions.

A. Only Case 1

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. Only Case 1

Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$ with $\tau_i=Y(1)-Y(0)>0$ a.s. and under conditional unconfoundedness

$E[Y\mid D,X]=m_{0}(X)+D\tau(X),\qquad m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X],\;
\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0\;\hbox{a.s.}$

The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection coefficient.

Case 1. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0),Y(1))$. Then 
$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation makes the intercept–slope projection the ATE,
so the sign is forced.

Case 2. $D\perp (Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$
The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ can be made
arbitrarily large and of either sign by letting $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$ be
monotone opposite to $m_{0}(X)$.  With $\tau>0$ small the marginal
difference can be $<0$.  $Y$ on $1,D$ is confounded.

Case 3. Regress $Y$ on $1,D,X$ linearly. Let $D_{\perp}=D-\operatorname{proj}_{1,X}D$
be the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$. 
$\beta_{3}=E[D_{\perp}Y]/E[D_{\perp}^{2}]
 =E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]/E[D_{\perp}^{2}]+E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]/E[D_{\perp}^{2}]$.
$E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]>0$ but $E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]=\operatorname{Cov}(D_{\perp},m_{0}(X))$
is generally non-zero.  $E[D_{\perp}\mid X]=p(X)-a-bX\neq0$ unless $p(\cdot)$
is linear in $X$, so the first term can dominate and be arbitrarily negative.
E.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$, $P(X)=1/3$, $p(0)=0.2,p(1)=0.8,p(2)=0.2$,
$m_{0}(x)=x^{3}$, $\tau(x)\equiv\varepsilon>0$ gives
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D)<0$ and $\beta_{3}<0$ even though
$E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ a.s.

Hence the conditional covariance $ \operatorname{Cov}(Y,D\mid X)=\tau(X)
\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X)>0$ is positive, but the linear projection on
$\{1,D,X\}$ is not the non-parametric partial covariance
$E[(D-E[D\mid X])Y]/E[(D-E[D\mid X])^{2}]$.  That latter weighted average
is $E[\tau(X)w(X)]/E[w(X)]>0$, but it is attained only if the linear
projection of $D$ on $X$ coincides with $E[D\mid X]$, i.e. if $p(X)$ is linear
in $X$, an extra parametric restriction the problem forbids.

Without parametric linearity the sign is protected only under unconditional
randomisation.  The marginal regression under conditional randomisation
and the linear $1,D,X$ regression under conditional randomisation can both
be signed the wrong way despite $\tau_i>0$ a.s.

3.text:
The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection coefficient.
Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$ and
$p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$.  Under conditional unconfoundedness
$E[Y\mid D,X]=m_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)$ with $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$.

* Case 1  $D\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0),Y(1))$.
$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)]-E[Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation is the ATE.

* Case 2  $D\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$.
$\beta_{2}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
 =E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]+E[\tau(X)\mid D=1]$.
The selection term can be made arbitrarily negative.  With $X\in\{0,1\}$,
$p(0)=0.9,\;p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(0)=0,\;m_{0}(1)=M$ and $\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=\varepsilon-0.8M<0$ for $M$ large.  The
marginal $Y\sim D$ slope is not sign protected.

* Case 3  $D\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ and $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+u$
in the $L^{2}$ sense.  Let $D_{\perp}=D-a-bX$ be the linear residual of $D$
on $1,X$.
$\beta_{3}=E[D_{\perp}Y]/E[D_{\perp}^{2}]
 =E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]/E[D_{\perp}^{2}] +E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]/E[D_{\perp}^{2}]$.
The second term is $>0$, the first term is $E[(p(X)-a-bX)m_{0}(X)]$.
It is zero only when $p(X)$ is linear in $X$.  With a non-linear $m_{0}$
and a non-linear propensity the linear residual of $D$ is not orthogonal
to $m_{0}(X)$.

E.g. $P(X=0)=P(X=1)=P(X=2)=1/3$, $p(0)=0.2,\;p(1)=0.8,\;p(2)=0.2$,
$m_{0}(x)=x^{3}$, $\tau(x)\equiv1$.  Then $E[D]=0.4$, $\operatorname{Cov}(D,X)=0$,
$D_{\perp}=D-0.4$, $\operatorname{Var}(D)=0.16$,
$\operatorname{Cov}(m_{0},D)=-0.4$, 
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D)=\operatorname{Cov}(m_{0},D)+\operatorname{Var}(D)=-0.24<0$,
so $\beta_{3}=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D)/\operatorname{Var}(D)<0$ even though
$E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=1>0$ for every $X$ and $\tau>0$ a.s.

The non-parametric residual $D-E[D\mid X]$ would give
$\beta^{np}=E[\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))]/E[p(X)(1-p(X))]>0$, but the
linear residual used by OLS on $1,D,X$ is not sign identified under
unconfoundedness alone.

Hence a strictly positive population OLS coefficient on $D$ is forced only
under unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1

4.text:
The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection on the space spanned
by the regressors.

*Case 1.* $D\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0),Y(1))$.  With $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s.,

$$
\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)]-E[Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0 ,
$$

the usual randomised ATE. Unconditional randomisation is sign protected.

*Case 2.* $D\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ but $D\not\perp\!\!\!\perp X$.
Write $m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ and
$p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$. Then

$$
E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau\mid D=1]
      +E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0] .
$$

The second term is selection on $X$.  With $p(X)$ decreasing in $m_{0}(X)$ it
can be made arbitrarily negative and dominate the positive
$E[\tau\mid D=1]$, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(0)=0$, $m_{0}(1)=M$, $\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$ gives
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=\varepsilon-0.8M<0$ for $M$ large.  The
uncontrolled $Y\sim1+D$ slope need not be $>0$ under conditional
randomisation.

*Case 3.*  $E[Y\mid X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$ with $\tau(X)>0$.  Let
$D_{\perp}=D-a_{0}-a_{1}X$ be the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$.  Then

$$
E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]+E[D_{\perp}D\,\tau(X)] .
$$

$E[D_{\perp}D\,\tau(X)]>0$ but

$$
E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]=E\big[(p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X)m_{0}(X)\big]
$$

is zero iff $p(X)$ is linear in $X$ or $m_{0}(X)$ is linear in $X$.  With a
non-linear $p(\cdot)$ and a non-linear $m_{0}(\cdot)$ the first term can be
made arbitrarily negative and dominate the second.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$,
$P(X)=1/3$, $p(0)=0.2$, $p(1)=0.8$, $p(2)=0.2$, $m_{0}(x)=x^{3}$,
$\tau\equiv1$, gives ${\rm Cov}(D,X)=0$ and

${\rm Cov}(Y,D)={\rm Cov}(m_{0},D)+\tau{\rm Var}(D)<0$,

so the linear projection $\beta_{D}={\rm Cov}(Y,D)/{\rm Var}(D)\approx-0.67<0$
although $E[Y(1)\mid X]-E[Y(0)\mid X]>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.
The non-parametric partial coefficient
$E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D\mid X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)]>0$ is sign protected,
but the ordinary linear projection on $1,D,X$ is not.

Hence a strictly positive population $D$ coefficient is guaranteed only
under unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1

public_text.7:
The population OLS coefficient is the coefficient of the $L^{2}$ linear
projection of $Y$ on the regressors that are included.

Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau=Y(1)-Y(0)>0$ a.s., and with conditional
unconfoundedness

$E[Y\mid X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$,      $m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$,
$\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$,               $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$.

Case 1. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0),Y(1))$.
\[
\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)]-E[Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0 .
\]
Unconditional randomisation is the ATE. The sign is forced.

Case 2. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ but in general
$D\not\perp\!\!\!\perp X$.  Then
\[
E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
 =E[\tau\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0].
\]
The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ can be made
arbitrarily negative by letting $p(X)$ be decreasing in $m_{0}(X)$. With
$\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$ arbitrarily small,
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=\varepsilon+{\rm bias}$ can be $<0$.  Conditional
unconfoundedness does not imply marginal unconfoundedness.

Case 3. The regression is the linear projection on $\{1,D,X\}$.
Put $D_{\perp}=D-\Pi_{1,X}D$, the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$.
Then
\[
\beta_{3}= \frac{{\rm Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})}{{\rm Var}(D_{\perp})}
        =\frac{E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]+E[\tau(X)D D_{\perp}]}
               {E[D_{\perp}^{2}]} .
\]
$E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]>0$ but $E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]=
E\big[(p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X)m_{0}(X)\big]$ is generally non-zero.
$D_{\perp}$ is orthogonal in $L^{2}$ to $1,X$ only, not to an arbitrary
function of $X$. With a non-linear $m_{0}(\cdot)$ and a non-linear
propensity $p(\cdot)$ the residual $p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X$ can be correlated
with $m_{0}(X)$ with a sign opposite to the positive $\tau$-term and with
arbitrarily large magnitude by scaling $m_{0}$. Hence
${\rm Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})$ can be made negative even though
${\rm Cov}(Y,D\mid X)=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D\mid X)>0$ pointwise.

E.g. $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$, $p(-1)=0.2$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.3$,
$m_{0}(x)=x^{2}$, $\tau(x)\equiv0.1>0$ gives $E[D_{\perp}Y]<0$ and
$\beta_{3}<0$.  The same construction works for any $c>0$.

Thus $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ a.s., but the best
linear predictor of $Y$ on $1,D,X$ is not the non-parametric
regression coefficient $E[\tau(X)w(X)]/E[w(X)]$ with $w(X)=p(X)(1-p(X))$.
The linear misspecification of $E[D\mid X]$ and $E[Y(0)\mid X]$ allows
sign reversal.

Positivity of the population $D$ coefficient is therefore guaranteed only
by unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can be negative with
$\tau_{i}>0$ a.s.

$$

$$
$E[\tau\mid D=1]>0$ but the selection term can dominate. With

$$
E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]+E[D_{\perp}D\,\tau(X)] .
$$
$E[D_{\perp}D\,\tau(X)]>0$ but $E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]=E[(p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X)m_{0}(X)]$
is the covariance of the non-linear part of the propensity with the
baseline. With non-linear $p(\cdot)$ and non-linear $m_{0}(\cdot)$ this term

the linear residual $D_{\perp}$ is negatively correlated with $m_{0}(X)$ and

for every $X$.

$E[(D-E[D\mid X])Y]/E[(D-E[D\mid X])^{2}]

D_{\perp}=D-a_{0}-a_{1}X
$$
the residual of $D$ from its linear projection on $1,X$, not from the

$$
E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]+E[D_{\perp}D\,\tau(X)] .
$$
$E[D_{\perp}D\,\tau(X)]>0$ but

public_text.1:
The population linear projection is what OLS estimates.

Write $Y = Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $\mu_0(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$,
$\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ and $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$, $v(X)=p(X)(1-p(X))>0$.
Under conditional unconfoundedness
$E[Y|D,X]=\mu_0(X)+D\,\tau(X)$ and ${\rm Cov}(Y,D|X)=\tau(X)v(X)>0$.

Case 1 $D\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0),Y(1))$.  Then
$$
\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)]-E[Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0
$$
is the ATE.  Sign is protected.

Case 2 $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))|X$ but $D\not\perp\!\!\!\perp X$.
$$
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau|D=1]+E[\mu_0(X)|D=1]-E[\mu_0(X)|D=0].
$$
The conditional mean difference $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$,
but the marginal difference contains the selection bias
$E[\mu_0(X)|D=1]-E[\mu_0(X)|D=0]$.  With $p(X)$ monotone opposite to
$\mu_0(X)$ the bias can dominate $\tau$.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$,
$p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $\mu_0(0)=0,\mu_0(1)=M$, $\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$,
gives $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=\varepsilon-0.8M<0$ for $M$ large.  The
uncontrolled $Y\sim1+D$ regression is not sign-protected.

Case 3.  Let $D_{\perp}=D-a_{0}-a_{1}X$ be the residual from the linear
projection of $D$ on $1,X$.  Then
$$
\beta_{3}= \frac{E[D_{\perp}Y]}{E[D_{\perp}^{2}]},\qquad
E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}\mu_0(X)]+E[\tau(X)D_{\perp}D].
$$
Now $E[D_{\perp}D|X]=p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X$ times $v(X)$ up to scale, so
$$
E[\tau(X)D_{\perp}D]=E\!\left[\tau(X) \bigl(p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X\bigr)
      v(X)\right]>0
$$
in the sense of a positive term, but
$$
E[D_{\perp}\mu_0(X)]=E\!\left[\bigl(p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X\bigr)\mu_0(X)\right]
$$
is generally non-zero.  Orthogonality $E[D_{\perp}\mu_0(X)]=0$ holds iff
$p(X)$ is linear in $X$, i.e. iff $E[D|X]$ lies in the span $\{1,X\}$.
With a non-linear propensity and a non-linear $\mu_0$ the first term can
be made arbitrarily negative.

E.g. $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equally likely, $p(-1)=0.2,p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.3$,
$\mu_0(x)=x^{2}$, $\tau(x)\equiv0.1$.  The linear projection of $D$ on
$1,X$ gives $D_{\perp}=D-\hat a_{0}-\hat a_{1}X$ with
$E[D_{\perp}\mu_0(X)]<0$ and $|E[D_{\perp}\mu_0(X)]|$ dominates
$E[\tau(X)D_{\perp}D]>0$, so $\beta_{3}<0$ despite
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ for every $X$.

In other words the non-parametric partial coefficient
$\beta^{*}=E[\tau(X)v(X)]/E[v(X)]>0$ is the sign-protected quantity,
and $\beta^{*}$ is what you get when $X$ is controlled non-parametrically,
i.e. with residual $D-E[D|X]$.  With the linear control $1,X$ the residual
is $D-\Pi_{1,X}D$ and orthogonality to $\mu_0(X)$ is lost.  Hence
unconfoundedness with a strictly positive individual effect does not
imply $\beta_{3}>0$.

Positivity of the population OLS coefficient on $D$ is therefore forced
only under unconditional randomisation.  Cases 2 and 3 are not sign-protected
without further functional-form restrictions.

The second term is selection on $X$.  With $p(X)$ decreasing in $m_{0}(X)$ it
can be made arbitrarily negative and dominate the positive
$E[\tau\mid D=1]$, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(0)=0$, $m_{0}(1)=M$, $\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$ gives
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=\varepsilon-0.8M<0$ for $M$ large.  The
uncontrolled $Y\sim1+D$ slope need not be $>0$ under conditional
randomisation.

*Case 3.*  $E[Y\mid X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$ with $\tau(X)>0$.  Let
$D_{\perp}=D-a_{0}-a_{1}X$ be the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$.  Then

$$
E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]+E[D_{\perp}D\,\tau(X)] .
$$

$E[D_{\perp}D\,\tau(X)]>0$ but

$$
E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]=E\big[(p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X)m_{0}(X)\big]
$$

is zero iff $p(X)$ is linear in $X$ or $m_{0}(X)$ is linear in $X$.  With a
non-linear $p(\cdot)$ and a non-linear $m_{0}(\cdot)$ the first term can be
made arbitrarily negative and dominate the second.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$,
$P(X)=1/3$, $p(0)=0.2$, $p(1)=0.8$, $p(2)=0.2$, $m_{0}(x)=x^{3}$,
$\tau\equiv1$, gives ${\rm Cov}(D,X)=0$ and

${\rm Cov}(Y,D)={\rm Cov}(m_{0},D)+\tau{\rm Var}(D)<0$,

so the linear projection $\beta_{D}={\rm Cov}(Y,D)/{\rm Var}(D)\approx-0.67<0$
although $E[Y(1)\mid X]-E[Y(0)\mid X]>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.
The non-parametric partial coefficient
$E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D\mid X)]/E[{\rm Var}(D\mid X)]>0$ is sign protected,
but the ordinary linear projection on $1,D,X$ is not.

Hence a strictly positive population $D$ coefficient is guaranteed only
under unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The potential outcomes set-up is $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$ with $\tau>0$ a.s., $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $m_0(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$, $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$, $v(X)=p(1-p)$.
Conditional unconfoundedness gives $E[Y|D,X]=m_0(X)+D\tau(X)$ and ${\rm Cov}(Y,D|X)=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)>0$ pointwise.

Case 1. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))$. Then $\beta_1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$. Unconditional randomisation is the ATE and sign is forced.

Case 2. $D\perp (Y(0),Y(1))|X$ but $D\not\perp X$ in general. 
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$ can be made arbitrarily negative by taking $p(X)$ decreasing in $m_0(X)$. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $m_0(0)=0$, $m_0(1)=M$, $\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$ gives $\beta_2=\varepsilon-0.8M<0$. Marginal $Y\sim1+D$ is not sign-protected.

Case 3. OLS on $1,D,X$ is the linear projection $\beta_3=E[D_{\perp}Y]/E[D_{\perp}^2]$ with $D_{\perp}=D-a_0-a_1X$, the residual of $D$ from its linear projection on $1,X$, not the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$. 
$E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}m_0(X)]+E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]$.
$E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]>0$, but $E[D_{\perp}m_0(X)]=E[(p(X)-a_0-a_1X)m_0(X)]$ is zero only if $p(X)$ is linear in $X$. With non-linear $p(\cdot)$ and non-linear $m_0(\cdot)$ the first term can be made arbitrarily negative and dominate the positive $\tau$ part. Example $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$, $p(-1)=0.2,p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.3$, $m_0(x)=x^2$, $\tau\equiv0.1$ gives $E[D_{\perp}Y]<0$, i.e. $\beta_3<0$ despite $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]>0$ a.s.
The sign-protected non-parametric partial effect is $E[\tau(X)v(X)]/E[v(X)]>0$, i.e. the coefficient obtained with residual $D-E[D|X]$, which is not the OLS coefficient with $X$ entered linearly. The linear misspecification breaks orthogonality to $m_0(X)$.

Thus positivity of the population OLS coefficient on $D$ is forced only by unconditional randomisation. Conditional randomisation protects the conditional covariance and protects the non-parametrically controlled coefficient, but does not protect the marginal $Y\sim D$ coefficient nor the linear $Y\sim1+D+X$ coefficient without additional linearity restrictions. The current round consensus is A. Only Case 1. Earlier dissent claiming Case 3 is sign-protected relied on the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$, not the linear residual used by OLS with a single linear term in $X$.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection coefficient.

Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $m_0(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$, $w(X)=p(X)(1-p(X))$.
Under conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y|D,X]=m_0(X)+D\tau(X)$ and ${\rm Cov}(Y,D|X)=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)>0$.

Case 1 $D\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0),Y(1))$. Then
$\beta_1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)]-E[Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation gives the ATE; sign is forced.

Case 2 $D\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0),Y(1))|X$.
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_0|D=1]-E[m_0|D=0]$ can be made arbitrarily negative by letting $p(X)$ decrease in $m_0(X)$. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $m_0(0)=0$, $m_0(1)=M$, $\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$ gives $\beta_2=\varepsilon-0.8M<0$ for large $M$. The marginal $Y\sim1+D$ regression is not sign protected.

Case 3 $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))|X$ and linear regression $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+\varepsilon$.
$\beta_3=E[D_\perp Y]/E[D_\perp^2]$ with $D_\perp=D-a_0-a_1X$ the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$.
$E[D_\perp Y]=E[D_\perp m_0(X)]+E[D_\perp D\tau(X)]$.
$E[D_\perp D\tau(X)]>0$, but $E[D_\perp m_0(X)]=E[(p(X)-a_0-a_1X)m_0(X)]$ is generally $\neq0$. It is zero iff $p(X)$ is linear in $X$, i.e. $E[D|X]\in {\rm span}\{1,X\}$. With a non-linear propensity and a non-linear $m_0$ the first term can dominate and be arbitrarily negative.

Example $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ each $1/3$, $p(0)=0.2$, $p(1)=0.8$, $p(2)=0.2$, $m_0(x)=x^3$, $\tau\equiv1$.
${\rm Cov}(D,X)=0$, $D_\perp=D-0.4$, ${\rm Cov}(m_0,D)=-0.4$, ${\rm Cov}(Y,D)=-0.24<0$, so $\beta_3<0$ despite $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ a.s. and $\tau_i>0$ a.s.

The sign-protected non-parametric partial effect is
$\beta^{np}=E[\tau(X)w(X)]/E[w(X)]>0$ with residual $D-E[D|X]$. That is obtained with fully non-parametric control for $X$, not with the linear control $1,X$. Under the stated no-parametric-assumptions restriction, the OLS coefficient with $X$ entered linearly is not sign identified.

Hence positivity of the population OLS coefficient on $D$ is forced only under unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can be negative even with $\tau_i>0$ a.s.

Current consensus in the room is A. Only Case 1. The earlier split between A and E is resolved by recognising the linear vs non-parametric residualisation issue for Case 3. Unresolved nuance remains about parametric linearity of $p(X)$ and $m_0(X)$ which would make Case 3 sign protected, but that is an extra restriction not allowed.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection onto the regressors actually included.

Case 1. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))$. Then with $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s.,
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation gives the mean difference = ATE and the sign is forced.

Case 2. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ but $D\not\perp\!\!\!\perp X$ in general.
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$ with $m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$.
The selection term can dominate. With $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(0)=0$, $m_{0}(1)=M$, $\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$,
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=\varepsilon-0.8M<0$ for $M$ large. So the $1+D$ projection can be negative.

Case 3. Under conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y|D,X]=m_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)$ with $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$.
Conditional covariance is ${\rm Cov}(Y,D|X)=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)>0$.
The OLS coefficient on $1,D,X$ is $\beta_{3}=E[D_{\perp}Y]/E[D_{\perp}^{2}]$ with $D_{\perp}=D-a_{0}-a_{1}X$, the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$.
$E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]+E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]$.
The second term is positive, the first term is $E[(p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X)m_{0}(X)]$.
It is zero iff $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$ is linear in $X$. With non-linear $p(\cdot)$ and non-linear $m_{0}(\cdot)$ the first term can be made arbitrarily negative and dominate the positive $\tau$ part.
E.g. $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equal mass, $p(-1)=0.2$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.3$, $m_{0}(x)=x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv0.1>0$ gives $E[D_{\perp}Y]<0$, $\beta_{3}<0$ despite $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise.

The non-parametric partial effect $E[\tau(X)w(X)]/E[w(X)]$, $w(X)=p(X)(1-p(X))>0$, is positive and is the coefficient obtained with the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$, i.e. with a fully non-parametric control for $X$. That is not the OLS coefficient with $X$ entered linearly. The earlier claims that Case 3 is sign-protected rely on that non-parametric residual.

Hence positivity of the population OLS $D$ coefficient is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can be made negative with $\tau_i>0$ a.s. under the stated no-parametric-restrictions beyond what is given.

Current belief: Only Case 1 must be positive, option A. Colleagues 1,2,3,4,6,7,8 in this round agree on A; the earlier dissenters who claimed Case 3 sign-protected with linear $X$ have shifted to the linear-misspecification argument.

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection coefficient.

Potential outcomes: Y = Y(0)+ D τ, τ_i = Y(1)-Y(0) >0 a.s., m0(X)=E[Y(0)|X], τ(X)=E[τ|X]>0, p(X)=P(D=1|X). Under conditional unconfoundedness D⊥Y(0),Y(1)|X ⇒ E[Y|X,D]=m0(X)+D τ(X), Cov(Y,D|X)=τ(X)Var(D|X)>0.

Case 1: D⊥Y(0),Y(1). Then β1 = E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)]-E[Y(0)]=E[τ]>0. Unconditional randomisation is sign protected. Agreed by all.

Case 2: D⊥Y(0),Y(1)|X but D not ⊥ X. 
β2 = E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ|D=1]+E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0].
Selection bias E[m0|X]|D=1 -E[m0|X]|D=0 can dominate the positive τ term. Example X∈{0,1}, p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1,m0(0)=0,m0(1)=M, τ≡ε>0 gives β2=ε-0.8M<0 for large M. So marginal Y∼D regression is not sign protected under conditional randomisation. All colleagues agree.

Case 3: regression Y on 1,D,X linearly. 
β3 = E[D⊥Y]/E[D⊥²] with D⊥ = D - a0 - a1 X = D - Π_lin(D|1,X). 
E[D⊥Y] = E[D⊥ m0(X)] + E[D⊥ D τ(X)].
E[D⊥ D τ(X)] >0 but E[D⊥ m0(X)] = E[(p(X)-a0-a1X)m0(X)] is generally ≠0. It is zero iff p(X) is linear in X. With non-linear p(·) and non-linear m0(·) it can be made arbitrarily negative and dominate the positive τ term.

Counterexample: X∈{0,1,2} P=1/3, p(0)=0.2,p(1)=0.8,p(2)=0.2, m0(x)=x³, τ≡1. Then Cov(D,X)=0 so D⊥=D-0.4, Var(D)=0.24, Cov(Y,D)=Cov(m0,D)+Var(D) = -0.4+0.24<0 ⇒ β3<0 ≈ -0.67. Same with X∈{-1,0,1}, p(-1)=0.2,p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.3, m0(x)=x², τ≡0.1 gives β3<0.

The non-parametric partial coefficient using residual D-E[D|X] is β*_np = E[τ(X)w(X)]/E[w(X)] >0 with w(X)=p(X)(1-p(X)). That is sign protected. Colleagues 4,5,7 in earlier rounds and 4,5,7 in this round claim this is the OLS coefficient with X included, i.e. they identify D⊥ with D-E[D|X]. That is a parametric linearity mistake: the linear projection residual is D-Π_lin(D|1,X) not D-E[D|X]. No parametric assumption on m0 or p is allowed.

Hence positivity is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can be negative despite τ_i>0 a.s. The only sign-protected case is Case 1, option A. Only Case 1 and Case 3 is the mistaken non-parametric linear-control view.

Disagreement persists about Case 3; current round majority 1,2,3,6,8 assert A, with 4,5,7 assert E. The sign reversal via non-linear m0 and non-linear propensity is the decisive correction.

7.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The problem is sign of the population linear projection coefficient on D when τ_i = Y(1)-Y(0)>0 a.s.

Case 1. D ⟂ (Y(0),Y(1)). Intercept–slope projection
β1 = E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)]-E[Y(0)]=E[τ]>0.
Unconditional randomisation gives the ATE, sign is forced.

Case 2. D ⟂ (Y(0),Y(1))|X but D is marginally dependent on X.
E[Y|D,X]=m0(X)+D τ(X), m0=E[Y(0)|X], τ(X)=E[τ|X]>0.
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ|D=1]+E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0].
The selection term can be made arbitrarily negative by letting p(X)=P(D=1|X) decrease in m0(X). With τ arbitrarily small and positive the marginal OLS slope β2 =E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0] can be <0. Conditional unconfoundedness does not imply marginal unconfoundedness.

Case 3. D ⟂ (Y(0),Y(1))|X and we project linearly on 1,D,X.
The relevant residual is D⊥ = D - Proj_{1,X} D, not D - E[D|X].
β3 = E[D⊥ Y]/E[D⊥²] = E[D⊥ m0(X)]/E[D⊥²] + E[D⊥ D τ(X)]/E[D⊥²].
E[D⊥ D τ(X)]>0, but E[D⊥ m0(X)]=E[(p(X)-a0-a1X) m0(X)] is generally ≠0.
It is zero only if p(X) is linear in X, i.e. E[D|X] lies in span{1,X}.
With non-linear m0(·) and non-linear p(·) the covariance of the linear residual of p(X) with m0(X) can be made arbitrarily negative and dominate the positive τ-term. E.g. X∈{-1,0,1}, p(-1)=0.2,p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.3, m0(x)=x², τ≡0.1 gives E[D⊥Y]<0 so β3<0.
The non-parametric partial coefficient
β* = E[τ(X) p(1-p)]/E[p(1-p)] >0,
which is the sign-protected quantity, is obtained with residual D-E[D|X], not with the linear residual D-Π_{1,X}D. Under unrestricted non-linear m0 and p the OLS coefficient on D with X entered linearly is not sign-identified.

Hence positivity of the individual effect is preserved only by unconditional randomisation. Conditional randomisation protects the conditional mean difference E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=τ(X)>0 but not the marginal OLS slope in Case 2 nor the linear partial coefficient in Case 3 under model misspecification.

Current belief: only Case 1 must be strictly positive in population; Cases 2 and 3 can be signed either way with τ_i>0 a.s. That is option A. Earlier round disagreement about Case 3 using the non-parametric residual is resolved in favour of the linear-projection argument.

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection on the actually included regressors. Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$, $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$, $v(X)=p(1-p)$.

Case 1. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0),Y(1))$.
$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation makes the intercept–slope projection the ATE; sign is forced. All colleagues agree.

Case 2. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$ generally.
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.
The conditional mean difference $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$, but the marginal difference contains selection bias $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$. With $p(X)$ monotone opposite to $m_{0}(X)$ the bias can dominate $\tau$. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(0)=0$, $m_{0}(1)=M$, $\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$ gives $\beta_{2}= \varepsilon-0.8M<0$ for large $M$. The uncontrolled $Y\sim1+D$ regression is not sign-protected.

Case 3. Projection on $\{1,D,X\}$: $\beta_{3}=E[D_{\perp}Y]/E[D_{\perp}^{2}]$ with $D_{\perp}=D-a_{0}-a_{1}X$, the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$, not the non-parametric residual $D-E[D\mid X]$.
$E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]+E[D_{\perp}D\,\tau(X)]$.
$E[D_{\perp}D\,\tau(X)]>0$ but $E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]=E[(p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X)m_{0}(X)]$ is generally non-zero. Orthogonality $E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]=0$ holds iff $p(X)$ is linear in $X$. With non-linear $p(\cdot)$ and non-linear $m_{0}(\cdot)$ the first term can be made arbitrarily negative and dominate the positive $\tau$ term.

Concrete counter-examples now in consensus: $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equally likely, $p(-1)=0.2$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.3$, $m_{0}(x)=x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv0.1$ gives $E[D_{\perp}Y]<0$ so $\beta_{3}<0$ despite $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]>0$ a.s. Also with ${\rm Cov}(D,X)=0$, e.g. $p(0)=0.2$, $p(1)=0.8$, $p(2)=0.2$, $m_{0}(x)=x^{3}$, $\tau\equiv1$, we get ${\rm Cov}(Y,D)<0$ and $\beta_{3}<0$.

The sign-protected quantity is the non-parametric partial effect
$\beta^{*}=E[\tau(X)v(X)]/E[v(X)]>0$, i.e. with residual $D-E[D\mid X]$. That is not the OLS coefficient with $X$ entered linearly. Linear misspecification of $E[D\mid X]$ and $E[Y(0)\mid X]$ allows sign reversal.

Hence positivity of $\tau_i>0$ a.s. forces a positive population OLS $D$ coefficient only under unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 are not sign-protected without further functional form restrictions.

Current belief: A. Only Case 1. Earlier disagreement about Case 3 – colleagues who argued for $E[(D-E[D\mid X])Y]/E[(D-E[D\mid X])^{2}]>0$ were using the non-parametric residual, not the linear residual required by the problem statement. The current round consensus resolves this in favour of A.

5.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The potential-outcome set-up is $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $m_0(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$, $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$, $w(X)=p(X)(1-p(X))>0$. Conditional unconfoundedness is $D\perp (Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ so $E[Y\mid D,X]=m_0(X)+D\tau(X)$ and ${\rm Cov}(Y,D\mid X)=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D\mid X)>0$.

Case 1 $D\perp (Y(0),Y(1))$. Linear projection on $\{1,D\}$ is the mean difference
$\beta_1=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$, unconditional randomisation forces sign.

Case 2 $D\perp (Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$. 
$\beta_2=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau\mid D=1]+E[m_0(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_0(X)\mid D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_0(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_0(X)\mid D=0]$ can dominate the positive $\tau$ term. With $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_0$ increasing, $\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$ arbitrarily small, $\beta_2=\varepsilon-0.8M<0$ is attainable. Sign not forced.

Case 3 regression $Y\sim1+D+X$ is linear projection onto span$\{1,D,X\}$. Write $D_{\perp}=D-a_0-a_1X$ for linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$. Then
$\beta_3=E[D_{\perp}Y]/E[D_{\perp}^2]$,
$E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}m_0(X)]+E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]$.
$E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]>0$ but $E[D_{\perp}m_0(X)]=E[(p(X)-a_0-a_1X)m_0(X)]$ is generally $\neq0$. Orthogonality $E[D_{\perp}m_0(X)]=0$ holds iff $p(X)$ is linear in $X$. With non-linear $p(\cdot)$ and non-linear $m_0(\cdot)$ the first term can be made arbitrarily negative and dominate the positive $\tau$ part, e.g. $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equal mass, $p(-1)=0.2,p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.3$, $m_0(x)=x^2$, $\tau\equiv0.1$ gives $E[D_{\perp}Y]<0$ so $\beta_3<0$ despite $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ a.s.

The non-parametric partial effect with residual $\tilde D=D-E[D\mid X]$ is
$\beta^{np}=E[\tau(X)w(X)]/E[w(X)]>0$, a positively weighted average of $\tau(X)$. That is sign-protected under unconfoundedness, and is what colleagues 4,5,7 previously invoked for Case 3. It is not the OLS coefficient with $X$ entered linearly, $D_{\perp}=D-\Pi_{1,X}D$. With a fully flexible control of $X$ Case 3 would be sign-protected; under the stated linear control it is not.

Hence the only case where positivity of $\tau_i>0$ a.s. forces a strictly positive population OLS coefficient on $D$ is unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can be negative under model misspecification.

Current round consensus is A. Only Case 1. Previously held nuance about non-parametric partial effect remains, explaining the earlier E arguments. No further unresolved issues for the stated linear specification.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The potential-outcome form is $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., and under conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y\mid X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)$ with $m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s., $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$. The population OLS coefficient is the $L^{2}$ linear projection on the regressors actually included.

Case 1. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))$. Then
$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation makes the intercept-slope projection the ATE; sign is forced.

Case 2. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ but $D\not\perp\!\!\!\perp X$ in general.
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ can be made arbitrarily large and of either sign by letting $p(X)$ be monotone opposite to $m_{0}(X)$. With $\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$ small the marginal difference can be $<0$, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(0)=0$, $m_{0}(1)=M$ gives $\varepsilon-0.8M<0$. The marginal $Y\sim1+D$ regression is not sign protected.

Case 3. With regressors $\{1,D,X\}$,
$\beta_{3}=E[D_{\perp}Y]/E[D_{\perp}^{2}]$ where $D_{\perp}=D-a_{0}-a_{1}X$ is the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$.
$E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]+E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]$.
$E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]>0$, but $E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]=E[(p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X)m_{0}(X)]$ is zero iff $p(\cdot)$ is linear in $X$ or $m_{0}(\cdot)$ is linear in $X$. Under conditional unconfoundedness alone $E[D_{\perp}\mid X]=p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X\neq0$ in general, so the first term can dominate and be arbitrarily negative by scaling $m_{0}$.
E.g. $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equiprobable, $p(-1)=0.2$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.3$, $m_{0}(x)=x^{2}$, $\tau(x)\equiv0.1>0$ gives $E[D_{\perp}Y]<0$ hence $\beta_{3}<0$ despite $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ a.s.

The non-parametric partial coefficient $E[\tau(X)w(X)]/E[w(X)]$, $w(X)=p(X)(1-p(X))>0$, obtained with residual $D-E[D\mid X]$, is $>0$, but that is not the OLS coefficient with $X$ entered linearly. Colleagues 4,5,7 obtain $\beta_{3}>0$ by effectively replacing $D_{\perp}$ with $D-E[D\mid X]$ i.e. by assuming $E[D\mid X]$ and $m_{0}(X)$ are linear in $X$, an extra parametric restriction forbidden by the problem.

Hence positivity of the individual effect is preserved by the unconditional mean difference, and by the non-parametric partial effect, but the linear projection on $1,D,X$ is not sign-identified under unconfoundedness alone. Sign reversal is possible in Cases 2 and 3.

Current best belief remains A. Only Case 1 is guaranteed positive in population OLS.

reflection_text.2:
The potential outcomes set-up is $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$ with $\tau>0$ a.s., $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $m_0(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$, $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$, $v(X)=p(1-p)$.
Conditional unconfoundedness gives $E[Y|D,X]=m_0(X)+D\tau(X)$ and ${\rm Cov}(Y,D|X)=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)>0$ pointwise.

Case 1. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))$. Then $\beta_1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$. Unconditional randomisation is the ATE and sign is forced.

Case 2. $D\perp (Y(0),Y(1))|X$ but $D\not\perp X$ in general. 
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$ can be made arbitrarily negative by taking $p(X)$ decreasing in $m_0(X)$. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $m_0(0)=0$, $m_0(1)=M$, $\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$ gives $\beta_2=\varepsilon-0.8M<0$. Marginal $Y\sim1+D$ is not sign-protected.

Case 3. OLS on $1,D,X$ is the linear projection $\beta_3=E[D_{\perp}Y]/E[D_{\perp}^2]$ with $D_{\perp}=D-a_0-a_1X$, the residual of $D$ from its linear projection on $1,X$, not the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$. 
$E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}m_0(X)]+E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]$.
$E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]>0$, but $E[D_{\perp}m_0(X)]=E[(p(X)-a_0-a_1X)m_0(X)]$ is zero only if $p(X)$ is linear in $X$. With non-linear $p(\cdot)$ and non-linear $m_0(\cdot)$ the first term can be made arbitrarily negative and dominate the positive $\tau$ part. Example $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$, $p(-1)=0.2,p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.3$, $m_0(x)=x^2$, $\tau\equiv0.1$ gives $E[D_{\perp}Y]<0$, i.e. $\beta_3<0$ despite $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]>0$ a.s.
The sign-protected non-parametric partial effect is $E[\tau(X)v(X)]/E[v(X)]>0$, i.e. the coefficient obtained with residual $D-E[D|X]$, which is not the OLS coefficient with $X$ entered linearly. The linear misspecification breaks orthogonality to $m_0(X)$.

Thus positivity of the population OLS coefficient on $D$ is forced only by unconditional randomisation. Conditional randomisation protects the conditional covariance and protects the non-parametrically controlled coefficient, but does not protect the marginal $Y\sim D$ coefficient nor the linear $Y\sim1+D+X$ coefficient without additional linearity restrictions. The current round consensus is A. Only Case 1. Earlier dissent claiming Case 3 is sign-protected relied on the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$, not the linear residual used by OLS with a single linear term in $X$.
reflection_text.3:
The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection coefficient.

Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $m_0(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$, $w(X)=p(X)(1-p(X))$.
Under conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y|D,X]=m_0(X)+D\tau(X)$ and ${\rm Cov}(Y,D|X)=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)>0$.

Case 1 $D\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0),Y(1))$. Then
$\beta_1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)]-E[Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation gives the ATE; sign is forced.

Case 2 $D\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0),Y(1))|X$.
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_0|D=1]-E[m_0|D=0]$ can be made arbitrarily negative by letting $p(X)$ decrease in $m_0(X)$. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $m_0(0)=0$, $m_0(1)=M$, $\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$ gives $\beta_2=\varepsilon-0.8M<0$ for large $M$. The marginal $Y\sim1+D$ regression is not sign protected.

Case 3 $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))|X$ and linear regression $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+\varepsilon$.
$\beta_3=E[D_\perp Y]/E[D_\perp^2]$ with $D_\perp=D-a_0-a_1X$ the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$.
$E[D_\perp Y]=E[D_\perp m_0(X)]+E[D_\perp D\tau(X)]$.
$E[D_\perp D\tau(X)]>0$, but $E[D_\perp m_0(X)]=E[(p(X)-a_0-a_1X)m_0(X)]$ is generally $\neq0$. It is zero iff $p(X)$ is linear in $X$, i.e. $E[D|X]\in {\rm span}\{1,X\}$. With a non-linear propensity and a non-linear $m_0$ the first term can dominate and be arbitrarily negative.

Example $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ each $1/3$, $p(0)=0.2$, $p(1)=0.8$, $p(2)=0.2$, $m_0(x)=x^3$, $\tau\equiv1$.
${\rm Cov}(D,X)=0$, $D_\perp=D-0.4$, ${\rm Cov}(m_0,D)=-0.4$, ${\rm Cov}(Y,D)=-0.24<0$, so $\beta_3<0$ despite $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=1>0$ a.s. and $\tau_i>0$ a.s.

The sign-protected non-parametric partial effect is
$\beta^{np}=E[\tau(X)w(X)]/E[w(X)]>0$ with residual $D-E[D|X]$. That is obtained with fully non-parametric control for $X$, not with the linear control $1,X$. Under the stated no-parametric-assumptions restriction, the OLS coefficient with $X$ entered linearly is not sign identified.

Hence positivity of the population OLS coefficient on $D$ is forced only under unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can be negative even with $\tau_i>0$ a.s.

Current consensus in the room is A. Only Case 1. The earlier split between A and E is resolved by recognising the linear vs non-parametric residualisation issue for Case 3. Unresolved nuance remains about parametric linearity of $p(X)$ and $m_0(X)$ which would make Case 3 sign protected, but that is an extra restriction not allowed.
reflection_text.6:
The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection onto the regressors actually included.

Case 1. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))$. Then with $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s.,
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation gives the mean difference = ATE and the sign is forced.

Case 2. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ but $D\not\perp\!\!\!\perp X$ in general.
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$ with $m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$.
The selection term can dominate. With $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(0)=0$, $m_{0}(1)=M$, $\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$,
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=\varepsilon-0.8M<0$ for $M$ large. So the $1+D$ projection can be negative.

Case 3. Under conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y|D,X]=m_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)$ with $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$.
Conditional covariance is ${\rm Cov}(Y,D|X)=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)>0$.
The OLS coefficient on $1,D,X$ is $\beta_{3}=E[D_{\perp}Y]/E[D_{\perp}^{2}]$ with $D_{\perp}=D-a_{0}-a_{1}X$, the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$.
$E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]+E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]$.
The second term is positive, the first term is $E[(p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X)m_{0}(X)]$.
It is zero iff $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$ is linear in $X$. With non-linear $p(\cdot)$ and non-linear $m_{0}(\cdot)$ the first term can be made arbitrarily negative and dominate the positive $\tau$ part.
E.g. $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equal mass, $p(-1)=0.2$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.3$, $m_{0}(x)=x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv0.1>0$ gives $E[D_{\perp}Y]<0$, $\beta_{3}<0$ despite $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise.

The non-parametric partial effect $E[\tau(X)w(X)]/E[w(X)]$, $w(X)=p(X)(1-p(X))>0$, is positive and is the coefficient obtained with the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$, i.e. with a fully non-parametric control for $X$. That is not the OLS coefficient with $X$ entered linearly. The earlier claims that Case 3 is sign-protected rely on that non-parametric residual.

Hence positivity of the population OLS $D$ coefficient is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can be made negative with $\tau_i>0$ a.s. under the stated no-parametric-restrictions beyond what is given.

Current belief: Only Case 1 must be positive, option A. Colleagues 1,2,3,4,6,7,8 in this round agree on A; the earlier dissenters who claimed Case 3 sign-protected with linear $X$ have shifted to the linear-misspecification argument.
reflection_text.4:
The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection coefficient.

Potential outcomes: Y = Y(0)+ D τ, τ_i = Y(1)-Y(0) >0 a.s., m0(X)=E[Y(0)|X], τ(X)=E[τ|X]>0, p(X)=P(D=1|X). Under conditional unconfoundedness D⊥Y(0),Y(1)|X ⇒ E[Y|X,D]=m0(X)+D τ(X), Cov(Y,D|X)=τ(X)Var(D|X)>0.

Case 1: D⊥Y(0),Y(1). Then β1 = E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)]-E[Y(0)]=E[τ]>0. Unconditional randomisation is sign protected. Agreed by all.

Case 2: D⊥Y(0),Y(1)|X but D not ⊥ X. 
β2 = E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ|D=1]+E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0].
Selection bias E[m0|X]|D=1 -E[m0|X]|D=0 can dominate the positive τ term. Example X∈{0,1}, p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1,m0(0)=0,m0(1)=M, τ≡ε>0 gives β2=ε-0.8M<0 for large M. So marginal Y∼D regression is not sign protected under conditional randomisation. All colleagues agree.

Case 3: regression Y on 1,D,X linearly. 
β3 = E[D⊥Y]/E[D⊥²] with D⊥ = D - a0 - a1 X = D - Π_lin(D|1,X). 
E[D⊥Y] = E[D⊥ m0(X)] + E[D⊥ D τ(X)].
E[D⊥ D τ(X)] >0 but E[D⊥ m0(X)] = E[(p(X)-a0-a1X)m0(X)] is generally ≠0. It is zero iff p(X) is linear in X. With non-linear p(·) and non-linear m0(·) it can be made arbitrarily negative and dominate the positive τ term.

Counterexample: X∈{0,1,2} P=1/3, p(0)=0.2,p(1)=0.8,p(2)=0.2, m0(x)=x³, τ≡1. Then Cov(D,X)=0 so D⊥=D-0.4, Var(D)=0.24, Cov(Y,D)=Cov(m0,D)+Var(D) = -0.4+0.24<0 ⇒ β3<0 ≈ -0.67. Same with X∈{-1,0,1}, p(-1)=0.2,p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.3, m0(x)=x², τ≡0.1 gives β3<0.

The non-parametric partial coefficient using residual D-E[D|X] is β*_np = E[τ(X)w(X)]/E[w(X)] >0 with w(X)=p(X)(1-p(X)). That is sign protected. Colleagues 4,5,7 in earlier rounds and 4,5,7 in this round claim this is the OLS coefficient with X included, i.e. they identify D⊥ with D-E[D|X]. That is a parametric linearity mistake: the linear projection residual is D-Π_lin(D|1,X) not D-E[D|X]. No parametric assumption on m0 or p is allowed.

Hence positivity is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can be negative despite τ_i>0 a.s. The only sign-protected case is Case 1, option A. Only Case 1 and Case 3 is the mistaken non-parametric linear-control view.

Disagreement persists about Case 3; current round majority 1,2,3,6,8 assert A, with 4,5,7 assert E. The sign reversal via non-linear m0 and non-linear propensity is the decisive correction.
reflection_text.7:
The problem is sign of the population linear projection coefficient on D when τ_i = Y(1)-Y(0)>0 a.s.

Case 1. D ⟂ (Y(0),Y(1)). Intercept–slope projection
β1 = E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)]-E[Y(0)]=E[τ]>0.
Unconditional randomisation gives the ATE, sign is forced.

Case 2. D ⟂ (Y(0),Y(1))|X but D is marginally dependent on X.
E[Y|D,X]=m0(X)+D τ(X), m0=E[Y(0)|X], τ(X)=E[τ|X]>0.
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ|D=1]+E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0].
The selection term can be made arbitrarily negative by letting p(X)=P(D=1|X) decrease in m0(X). With τ arbitrarily small and positive the marginal OLS slope β2 =E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0] can be <0. Conditional unconfoundedness does not imply marginal unconfoundedness.

Case 3. D ⟂ (Y(0),Y(1))|X and we project linearly on 1,D,X.
The relevant residual is D⊥ = D - Proj_{1,X} D, not D - E[D|X].
β3 = E[D⊥ Y]/E[D⊥²] = E[D⊥ m0(X)]/E[D⊥²] + E[D⊥ D τ(X)]/E[D⊥²].
E[D⊥ D τ(X)]>0, but E[D⊥ m0(X)]=E[(p(X)-a0-a1X) m0(X)] is generally ≠0.
It is zero only if p(X) is linear in X, i.e. E[D|X] lies in span{1,X}.
With non-linear m0(·) and non-linear p(·) the covariance of the linear residual of p(X) with m0(X) can be made arbitrarily negative and dominate the positive τ-term. E.g. X∈{-1,0,1}, p(-1)=0.2,p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.3, m0(x)=x², τ≡0.1 gives E[D⊥Y]<0 so β3<0.
The non-parametric partial coefficient
β* = E[τ(X) p(1-p)]/E[p(1-p)] >0,
which is the sign-protected quantity, is obtained with residual D-E[D|X], not with the linear residual D-Π_{1,X}D. Under unrestricted non-linear m0 and p the OLS coefficient on D with X entered linearly is not sign-identified.

Hence positivity of the individual effect is preserved only by unconditional randomisation. Conditional randomisation protects the conditional mean difference E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=τ(X)>0 but not the marginal OLS slope in Case 2 nor the linear partial coefficient in Case 3 under model misspecification.

Current belief: only Case 1 must be strictly positive in population; Cases 2 and 3 can be signed either way with τ_i>0 a.s. That is option A. Earlier round disagreement about Case 3 using the non-parametric residual is resolved in favour of the linear-projection argument.
reflection_text.1:
The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection on the actually included regressors. Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$, $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$, $v(X)=p(1-p)$.

Case 1. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0),Y(1))$.
$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation makes the intercept–slope projection the ATE; sign is forced. All colleagues agree.

Case 2. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$ generally.
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.
The conditional mean difference $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$, but the marginal difference contains selection bias $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$. With $p(X)$ monotone opposite to $m_{0}(X)$ the bias can dominate $\tau$. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(0)=0$, $m_{0}(1)=M$, $\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$ gives $\beta_{2}= \varepsilon-0.8M<0$ for large $M$. The uncontrolled $Y\sim1+D$ regression is not sign-protected.

Case 3. Projection on $\{1,D,X\}$: $\beta_{3}=E[D_{\perp}Y]/E[D_{\perp}^{2}]$ with $D_{\perp}=D-a_{0}-a_{1}X$, the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$, not the non-parametric residual $D-E[D\mid X]$.
$E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]+E[D_{\perp}D\,\tau(X)]$.
$E[D_{\perp}D\,\tau(X)]>0$ but $E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]=E[(p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X)m_{0}(X)]$ is generally non-zero. Orthogonality $E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]=0$ holds iff $p(X)$ is linear in $X$. With non-linear $p(\cdot)$ and non-linear $m_{0}(\cdot)$ the first term can be made arbitrarily negative and dominate the positive $\tau$ term.

Concrete counter-examples now in consensus: $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equally likely, $p(-1)=0.2$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.3$, $m_{0}(x)=x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv0.1$ gives $E[D_{\perp}Y]<0$ so $\beta_{3}<0$ despite $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]>0$ a.s. Also with ${\rm Cov}(D,X)=0$, e.g. $p(0)=0.2$, $p(1)=0.8$, $p(2)=0.2$, $m_{0}(x)=x^{3}$, $\tau\equiv1$, we get ${\rm Cov}(Y,D)<0$ and $\beta_{3}<0$.

The sign-protected quantity is the non-parametric partial effect
$\beta^{*}=E[\tau(X)v(X)]/E[v(X)]>0$, i.e. with residual $D-E[D\mid X]$. That is not the OLS coefficient with $X$ entered linearly. Linear misspecification of $E[D\mid X]$ and $E[Y(0)\mid X]$ allows sign reversal.

Hence positivity of $\tau_i>0$ a.s. forces a positive population OLS $D$ coefficient only under unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 are not sign-protected without further functional form restrictions.

Current belief: A. Only Case 1. Earlier disagreement about Case 3 – colleagues who argued for $E[(D-E[D\mid X])Y]/E[(D-E[D\mid X])^{2}]>0$ were using the non-parametric residual, not the linear residual required by the problem statement. The current round consensus resolves this in favour of A.
reflection_text.5:
The potential-outcome set-up is $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $m_0(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$, $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$, $w(X)=p(X)(1-p(X))>0$. Conditional unconfoundedness is $D\perp (Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ so $E[Y\mid D,X]=m_0(X)+D\tau(X)$ and ${\rm Cov}(Y,D\mid X)=\tau(X){\rm Var}(D\mid X)>0$.

Case 1 $D\perp (Y(0),Y(1))$. Linear projection on $\{1,D\}$ is the mean difference
$\beta_1=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$, unconditional randomisation forces sign.

Case 2 $D\perp (Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$. 
$\beta_2=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau\mid D=1]+E[m_0(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_0(X)\mid D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_0(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_0(X)\mid D=0]$ can dominate the positive $\tau$ term. With $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $m_0$ increasing, $\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$ arbitrarily small, $\beta_2=\varepsilon-0.8M<0$ is attainable. Sign not forced.

Case 3 regression $Y\sim1+D+X$ is linear projection onto span$\{1,D,X\}$. Write $D_{\perp}=D-a_0-a_1X$ for linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$. Then
$\beta_3=E[D_{\perp}Y]/E[D_{\perp}^2]$,
$E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}m_0(X)]+E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]$.
$E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]>0$ but $E[D_{\perp}m_0(X)]=E[(p(X)-a_0-a_1X)m_0(X)]$ is generally $\neq0$. Orthogonality $E[D_{\perp}m_0(X)]=0$ holds iff $p(X)$ is linear in $X$. With non-linear $p(\cdot)$ and non-linear $m_0(\cdot)$ the first term can be made arbitrarily negative and dominate the positive $\tau$ part, e.g. $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equal mass, $p(-1)=0.2,p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.3$, $m_0(x)=x^2$, $\tau\equiv0.1$ gives $E[D_{\perp}Y]<0$ so $\beta_3<0$ despite $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ a.s.

The non-parametric partial effect with residual $\tilde D=D-E[D\mid X]$ is
$\beta^{np}=E[\tau(X)w(X)]/E[w(X)]>0$, a positively weighted average of $\tau(X)$. That is sign-protected under unconfoundedness, and is what colleagues 4,5,7 previously invoked for Case 3. It is not the OLS coefficient with $X$ entered linearly, $D_{\perp}=D-\Pi_{1,X}D$. With a fully flexible control of $X$ Case 3 would be sign-protected; under the stated linear control it is not.

Hence the only case where positivity of $\tau_i>0$ a.s. forces a strictly positive population OLS coefficient on $D$ is unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can be negative under model misspecification.

Current round consensus is A. Only Case 1. Previously held nuance about non-parametric partial effect remains, explaining the earlier E arguments. No further unresolved issues for the stated linear specification.
reflection_text.8:
The potential-outcome form is $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., and under conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y\mid X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)$ with $m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ a.s., $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$. The population OLS coefficient is the $L^{2}$ linear projection on the regressors actually included.

Case 1. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))$. Then
$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation makes the intercept-slope projection the ATE; sign is forced.

Case 2. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ but $D\not\perp\!\!\!\perp X$ in general.
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$ can be made arbitrarily large and of either sign by letting $p(X)$ be monotone opposite to $m_{0}(X)$. With $\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$ small the marginal difference can be $<0$, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(0)=0$, $m_{0}(1)=M$ gives $\varepsilon-0.8M<0$. The marginal $Y\sim1+D$ regression is not sign protected.

Case 3. With regressors $\{1,D,X\}$,
$\beta_{3}=E[D_{\perp}Y]/E[D_{\perp}^{2}]$ where $D_{\perp}=D-a_{0}-a_{1}X$ is the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$.
$E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]+E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]$.
$E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]>0$, but $E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]=E[(p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X)m_{0}(X)]$ is zero iff $p(\cdot)$ is linear in $X$ or $m_{0}(\cdot)$ is linear in $X$. Under conditional unconfoundedness alone $E[D_{\perp}\mid X]=p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X\neq0$ in general, so the first term can dominate and be arbitrarily negative by scaling $m_{0}$.
E.g. $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equiprobable, $p(-1)=0.2$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.3$, $m_{0}(x)=x^{2}$, $\tau(x)\equiv0.1>0$ gives $E[D_{\perp}Y]<0$ hence $\beta_{3}<0$ despite $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ a.s.

The non-parametric partial coefficient $E[\tau(X)w(X)]/E[w(X)]$, $w(X)=p(X)(1-p(X))>0$, obtained with residual $D-E[D\mid X]$, is $>0$, but that is not the OLS coefficient with $X$ entered linearly. Colleagues 4,5,7 obtain $\beta_{3}>0$ by effectively replacing $D_{\perp}$ with $D-E[D\mid X]$ i.e. by assuming $E[D\mid X]$ and $m_{0}(X)$ are linear in $X$, an extra parametric restriction forbidden by the problem.

Hence positivity of the individual effect is preserved by the unconditional mean difference, and by the non-parametric partial effect, but the linear projection on $1,D,X$ is not sign-identified under unconfoundedness alone. Sign reversal is possible in Cases 2 and 3.

Current best belief remains A. Only Case 1 is guaranteed positive in population OLS.

A. Only Case 1

The population OLS coefficient is the linear projection coefficient on the regressors that are actually included.

Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$ and $p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$.  Under conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y\mid D,X]=m_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)$.

Case 1. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))$.
$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation makes the intercept-slope projection the ATE and the sign is forced.

Case 2. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$.
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$.
The conditional mean difference $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$, but the marginal difference contains the selection bias $E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0]$. With $p(X)$ monotone opposite to $m_{0}(X)$ the bias can dominate $\tau$, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(0)=0$, $m_{0}(1)=M$, $\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$ gives $\beta_{2}=\varepsilon-0.8M<0$ for large $M$.

Case 3. With $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+u$ in $L^{2}$ let $D_{\perp}=D-a_{0}-a_{1}X$ be the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$. Then
$\beta_{3}=E[D_{\perp}Y]/E[D_{\perp}^{2}]$, 
$E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]+E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]$.
$E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]>0$ but $E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]=E[(p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X)m_{0}(X)]\neq0$ in general. Orthogonality to $m_{0}(X)$ holds iff $p(X)$ is linear in $X$. With non-linear $p(\cdot)$ and non-linear $m_{0}(\cdot)$ the first term can be made arbitrarily negative and dominate the positive $\tau$ term, e.g. $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equally likely, $p(-1)=0.2$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.3$, $m_{0}(x)=x^{2}$, $\tau\equiv0.1$ gives $E[D_{\perp}Y]<0$ and $\beta_{3}<0$ despite $\tau(X)>0$ a.s.

The sign-protected quantity is the non-parametric partial effect $E[\tau(X)v(X)]/E[v(X)]>0$ with residual $D-E[D\mid X]$, not the linear residual $D-\Pi_{1,X}D$. With only the linear control $1,X$ the OLS $D$ coefficient can reverse sign. Positivity is forced only under unconditional randomisation.

2.text:

Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$ with $\tau>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$,

$E[Y|D,X]=m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X)$,

arbitrarily negative by letting $p(X)$ decrease in $m_{0}(X)$.
E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(0)=0$, $m_{0}(1)=M$,
$\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$ gives $\beta_{2}=\varepsilon-0.8M<0$ for $M$ big.

$\beta_{3}=E[D_{\perp}Y]/E[D_{\perp}^{2}]$ with $D_{\perp}=D-a_{0}-a_{1}X$ the
linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$. Then

$E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]+E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]$,

$E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]>0$ but $E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]=
E[(p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X)m_{0}(X)]$ is zero iff $p(X)$ is linear in $X$.

3.text:
The population OLS coefficient is the $L^{2}$ linear projection coefficient.

$$E[Y\mid D,X]=m_{0}(X)+D\,\tau(X),\qquad

$$\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)]-E[Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0,$$

$$
E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]
-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0].
$$
The selection term can be made arbitrarily negative by letting $p(X)$
decrease in $m_{0}(X)$.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$,

$\beta_{3}=E[D_{\perp}Y]/E[D_{\perp}^{2}]$ with
$D_{\perp}=D-a_{0}-a_{1}X$ the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$.
$$
E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]+E[D_{\perp}D\,\tau(X)] .

$E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]=E[(p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X)m_{0}(X)]$ is $0$ iff

E.g. $X\in\{0,1,2\}$ each $1/3$, $p(0)=0.2,p(1)=0.8,p(2)=0.2$,

5.text:

$$
\beta_3=\frac{E[D_{\perp}Y]}{E[D_{\perp}^2]},\qquad
E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}m_0(X)]+E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)] .
$$

7.text:

The population OLS coefficient is the $L^{2}$ linear projection on the set of regressors that are actually included, not the non-parametric conditional mean.

Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$,
$p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$ and $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$. Under conditional
unconfoundedness $E[Y\mid D,X]=m_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)$ and
${\rm Cov}(Y,D\mid X)=\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))>0$.

Case 1. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))$. Then $D\perp\!\!\!\perp X$ and
\[
\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)]-E[Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0 .
\]
Unconditional randomisation is the ATE, so the $1+D$ linear projection is
strictly positive.

Case 2. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ but $D\not\perp\!\!\!\perp X$ in
general.
\[
E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0].
\]
The selection term can dominate. With $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(0)=0,m_{0}(1)=M$, $\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$,
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=\varepsilon-0.8M<0$ for $M$ large. The marginal
$Y\sim1+D$ slope is not sign protected.

Case 3. The population coefficient from $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+u$,
$E[uD]=E[uX]=0$, is
\[
\beta_{3}= \frac{E[D_{\perp}Y]}{E[D_{\perp}^{2}]},\qquad 
D_{\perp}=D-a_{0}-a_{1}X ,
\]
the residual of $D$ from its linear projection on $1,X$.
\[
E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]+E[D_{\perp}D\,\tau(X)] ,
\]
with $E[D_{\perp}D\,\tau(X)]>0$ but
\[
E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]=E\big[(p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X)m_{0}(X)\big]
\]
zero iff $p(X)$ is linear in $X$. With a non-linear propensity and a
non-linear $m_{0}$ the first term can be made arbitrarily negative.
E.g. $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equal mass, $p(-1)=0.2,p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.3$,

$E[\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))]/E[p(X)(1-p(X))]>0$, obtained with residual
$D-E[D\mid X]$. With the linear residual $D-\Pi_{1,X}D$ orthogonality to

public_text.6:
The population OLS coefficient is the $L^{2}$ linear projection on the set of regressors that are actually included, not the non-parametric conditional mean.

Write $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$,
$p(X)=P(D=1\mid X)$ and $\tau(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$. Under conditional
unconfoundedness $E[Y\mid D,X]=m_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)$ and
${\rm Cov}(Y,D\mid X)=\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))>0$.

Case 1. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))$. Then $D\perp\!\!\!\perp X$ and
\[
\beta_{1}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[Y(1)]-E[Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0 .
\]
Unconditional randomisation is the ATE, so the $1+D$ linear projection is
strictly positive.

Case 2. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ but $D\not\perp\!\!\!\perp X$ in
general.
\[
E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau\mid D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)\mid D=0].
\]
The selection term can dominate. With $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$,
$m_{0}(0)=0,m_{0}(1)=M$, $\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$,
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=\varepsilon-0.8M<0$ for $M$ large. The marginal
$Y\sim1+D$ slope is not sign protected.

Case 3. The population coefficient from $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+u$,
$E[uD]=E[uX]=0$, is
\[
\beta_{3}= \frac{E[D_{\perp}Y]}{E[D_{\perp}^{2}]},\qquad 
D_{\perp}=D-a_{0}-a_{1}X ,
\]
the residual of $D$ from its linear projection on $1,X$.
\[
E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]+E[D_{\perp}D\,\tau(X)] ,
\]
with $E[D_{\perp}D\,\tau(X)]>0$ but
\[
E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]=E\big[(p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X)m_{0}(X)\big]
\]
zero iff $p(X)$ is linear in $X$. With a non-linear propensity and a
non-linear $m_{0}$ the first term can be made arbitrarily negative.
E.g. $X\in\{-1,0,1\}$ equal mass, $p(-1)=0.2,p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.3$,
$m_{0}(x)=x^{2},\tau\equiv0.1>0$ gives $E[D_{\perp}Y]<0$, i.e. $\beta_{3}<0$,
although $E[Y\mid D=1,X]-E[Y\mid D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ pointwise.

The sign-protected quantity is the non-parametric partial coefficient
$E[\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))]/E[p(X)(1-p(X))]>0$, obtained with residual
$D-E[D\mid X]$. With the linear residual $D-\Pi_{1,X}D$ orthogonality to
$m_{0}(X)$ is lost. Hence under the stated non-parametric restrictions
positivity of the OLS $D$ coefficient is forced only under unconditional
randomisation.

A. Only Case 1

Case 2. $D\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y(0),Y(1))\mid X$ but $D\not\perp X$ generally.

$\beta_{3}=E[D_{\perp}Y]/E[D_{\perp}^{2}]$, $E[D_{\perp}Y]=E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]+E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]$.
$E[D_{\perp}D\tau(X)]>0$ but $E[D_{\perp}m_{0}(X)]=E[(p(X)-a_{0}-a_{1}X)m_{0}(X)]$ is zero iff $p(X)$ is linear in $X$. With non-linear $p(\cdot)$ and non-linear $m_{0}(\cdot)$ the first term can be made arbitrarily negative and dominate.

With $\tau\equiv\varepsilon>0$ small the marginal difference can be $<0$, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, $m_{0}(0)=0$, $m_{0}(1)=M$ gives $\varepsilon-0.8M<0$. Case 3. With regressors $\{1,D,X\}$,

Current best belief remains A. Only Case 1 is guaranteed positive in population OLS.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The population OLS coefficient is the L2 linear projection on the regressors actually included.

Write Y = Y(0)+D τ, τ_i>0 a.s., m0(X)=E[Y(0)|X], τ(X)=E[τ|X]>0, p(X)=P(D=1|X). Under conditional unconfoundedness E[Y|D,X]=m0(X)+D τ(X) and Cov(Y,D|X)=τ(X)Var(D|X)>0.

Case 1 D ⟂⟂ (Y(0),Y(1)).
β1 = E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[τ]>0.
Unconditional randomisation makes the 1+D projection the ATE, sign forced.

Case 2 D ⟂⟂ (Y(0),Y(1))|X.
β2 = E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ|D=1]+E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0].
Selection term can dominate. E.g. X∈{0,1}, p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1, m0(0)=0,m0(1)=M, τ≡ε>0 gives β2= ε-0.8M<0 for large M. Marginal 1+D is not sign protected.
